title: The Days of Awe
hookLine: ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur for making amends

cards: Two dates circled on a kitchen calendar. Next to the first, someone has drawn a little ram's horn. Next to the second, one word: fast.
Between them, the squares are full of small notes. Call Mom. Coffee with Dan.
Write to Mr. Levin. Return the drill.
It looks like an ordinary to-do list. It isn't. It's a list of people.

teach.h: THE FIRST DAY AND THE TENTH.
teach.b: First, the calendar. Leviticus sets the two days. In the King James words: "In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation."
That's the day Jews call Rosh Hashanah, the new year. Then: "Also on the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a day of atonement." Yom Kippur.
From the first day to the tenth: ten days. In Hebrew they're the Yamim Noraim, the Days of Awe. Second, the picture.
Tradition says, in a teaching in the Talmud, that on the new year the books are opened, and on the Day of Atonement they're sealed. Those in between have until then.
It's an image, and readers hold it in different ways, but it gives the days their feel: a door that's open, and won't stay open forever. Third, the work.
A prayer in the liturgy for these days names three things that turn aside the harsh decree: repentance, prayer and charity.
Fourth, this whole week in one season. Forgiveness. The turn back.
Maimonides' four steps. Asking the person first. Joseph weeping.

Joseph and Esau are read at other times of the year, but the turning, the steps and the asking all come due in these ten days: the apology that's been waiting, the call you keep putting off, made inside a window with a closing date.

how: During the Days of Awe, Jews pray special prayers, hear the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, give charity, and seek out people they have wronged to ask forgiveness before Yom Kippur.

games.q: it's the Days of Awe. there's an apology you've put off all year. what does the season ask?
o: make it now, inside the ten days.
games.why: the ten days are set aside for teshuvah and for going to people you've wronged before Yom Kippur.

practice: Open a blank page in your mind and let names arrive, one at a time, of people you owe something: an apology, an overdue thank-you, a call, a thing to return.
Don't judge or rank the list; when no more come, look it over once, and give it a closing date ten days away. If you pray, you can hold the list in your prayer, in your own words.
